This manual covered a wide-range of disaster and disruption scenarios. The manual is based off both past disasters in St. Louis County (largest county east of the Mississippi River) and what emergency government planners see as future hazards based upon a changing climate. Using this manual as a foundation, the CIT codified scenarios to advance to project partner Ecolibrium3 for community-based participatory research, and worked as a team to identify one large disruption scenario, with cascading events, that could be used to develop a tabletop exercise. The City of Duluth connected with 19 organization and departments on the state, regional, and local level. These organizations provided 40 people to participate in two tabletop exercises. The first was held with the CIT, government representatives, and limited community-based organizations. The tabletop exercise was then repeated with a focus on participation by community-based organizations. During the second tabletop exercise, participants were asked to create personas of individuals they serve, to better 11 identify most at-risk or vulnerable individuals that may need a different level of resilience and/or response during a grid outage situation. The exercise scenario and progression of events included (Figure 4): From the tabletop conversations and debriefing, several important factors were identified to inform the CIT’s development of a site rubric, selection of top potential renewable development sites, and formation of the Community Stakeholder Group’s (CSG) community-based research plan. A major realization was the disconnect experienced between emergency government and community-based organizations in the scenario. Community-based organizations were less familiar with the processes and thresholds that are used by emergency management to determine government response. It was clear that power outages would continue to be addressed until power was restored to all affected households, however, the scenario included minor basement flooding for a portion of the community. Community-based organizations reflected surprise that unless a certain damage threshold was met, impacted community members would need to address damage on their own. Better understanding these thresholds and how the different disaster scenarios could impact various households became a focus of community-based research under Task 2.0.
